To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PTEN is a critical regulator of lymphomagenis, and that its loss in T cell malignancies is associated with the development of TCR-dependent c-myc translocations.

PTEN loss in T cell lymphomas is associated with c-myc overexpression, that T cell lymphoma is dependent on TCR and Notch pathways to drive c-myc over-expression, that TCR recombination is not required for T cell lymphoma, that PTEN-deficiency in T cells can cause autoimmunity, and that TCR recombined mature T cells are not sufficient to cause lymphoma but are sufficient for autoimmune disease.
PTEN loss induces lymphomas and autoimmunity, and that these diseases have distinct etiology, are separable, and mediated by T cell progenitors of different developmental stages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the PTEN tumor suppressor gene in T cell lymphoma.
understanding the molecular basis of T-cell lymphomagenesis.
the role of the tumor suppressor PTEN in the pathogenesis of T cell lymphomas and autoimmune disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PTEN loss in T cell malignancy can drive lymphomagenesis by multiple distinct molecular pathways, depending upon the developmental stage and environment of T cells.
PTEN plays distinct and separable roles in T cell lymphoma development and autoimmunity.

PTEN deficiency in T cells leads to the development of T cell lymphomas and autoimmunity, but that these diseases have different pathogenic mechanisms and are mediated by T cells at different stages of development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PTEN is a potent suppressor of lymphomagenisis in the thymus but is dispensable for T cell-mediated autoimmune disease.
loss of Pten in the thymus induces lymphoma, and loss of Pten outside the thymus leads to lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, but neither is sufficient to induce the other.
PTEN loss can drive T cell malignancies in a TCR- and Notch-dependent fashion, whereas PTEN deficiency in mature T cells is sufficient for autoimmunity, but not lymphomagenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PTEN loss in T cells is a potent driver of lymphomogenesis in the thymus.
PTEN loss in T cells is sufficient to drive the development of two distinct T cell diseases: lymphomas and autoimmune diseases.
PTEN is required to prevent the development of lymphomas in the thymus, and that this is due to its role in regulating the expression of the c-mys oncogene in thymocytes.
